Emergency shortwave radio: what to listen to when everything else is down

Shortwave radio doesn't depend on the internet, cell towers or the local grid for reception, which is why preppers keep one in the kit. This guide shows what to listen to, when, and how to test your radio before you need it. Everything here is receive-only; no license needed.

Tonight's full listening guide

Be realistic. International shortwave broadcasters are not emergency services, and no station promises to report on your local emergency. Shortwave is a backup source: news from outside your area, accurate time, and space-weather alerts when other channels are down. Local AM/FM and NOAA Weather Radio come first for local warnings.

Step 1: Test your radio now

  1. Put in fresh batteries and set the radio to AM mode (shortwave broadcasts and WWV are AM).
  2. Tune to 10 MHz (10000 kHz) or 5 MHz (5000 kHz) and listen for WWV: a steady tick and a voice announcing the time.
  3. No signal? Try the other WWV frequencies below. Which one works depends on time of day.
  4. Clip 20 feet (6 m) or more of wire to the telescopic antenna, run it outside or along a window, and compare the difference.

Step 2: Know the time-signal stations

These transmit around the clock and are the easiest way to prove your radio works. Frequencies per NIST (WWV/WWVH) and the National Research Council (CHU).

StationFrequencies (MHz)What you hear
WWV — Fort Collins, Colorado2.5 · 5 · 10 · 15 · 20Voice time announcement (UTC), tones, geophysical (space-weather) alerts, Atlantic/Pacific storm information
WWVH — Kauai, Hawaii2.5 · 5 · 10 · 15Same services from the Pacific
CHU — Ottawa, Canada3.330 · 7.850 · 14.670Time signals in English and French

Step 3: Pick the band for the time of day

WhenTry (MHz)Why
Night3 – 7Lower bands carry farthest after dark
Evening / overnight7 – 11Strong at dusk and into the night
Daytime13 – 21Higher bands need sunlight to work

Conditions change daily with the sun. Our propagation page shows current space weather.

Radio check (every 3 months)

  • Fresh batteries in the radio, spares stored separately
  • AM mode: found WWV on 5, 10 or 15 MHz
  • 20+ ft of wire and clip ready
  • Local AM/FM and NOAA Weather Radio checked
  • This card reprinted after each season change (late March / late October)

Do I need a license to listen to shortwave radio?

No. In the United States you don't need a license to listen to shortwave or any other radio broadcast. A license is only required to transmit, for example on the amateur (ham) bands.

Will shortwave work if the power, internet and cell service are down?

Receiving does not depend on the internet or cell towers. A battery radio can keep receiving as long as stations are on the air, and the big international transmitters run on their own power systems. Nothing is guaranteed in a regional disaster, so also keep local AM/FM and NOAA Weather Radio (VHF, not shortwave) in your kit.

Which shortwave stations are best in an emergency?

Start with WWV/WWVH (time, space-weather alerts and storm information) to confirm your radio and antenna work, then try English-language international broadcasters aimed at North America. The tables on this page are rebuilt daily from the broadcast schedule.

What time of day is best for shortwave?

After dark the lower bands (about 3–7 MHz) carry the farthest. Mid-evening through the night 7–10 MHz is strong, and during the day the higher bands (about 13–21 MHz) work best. A geomagnetic storm can black out all of them.

Can I talk to people on shortwave in an emergency?

Shortwave broadcast bands are receive-only for the public. Two-way HF communication needs an amateur radio license, apart from a few limited services. Many people get a ham license before they need it.

What kind of radio and antenna do I need?

Any radio that covers shortwave in AM mode will work. Fresh batteries and about 20 feet (6 m) or more of wire clipped to the telescopic antenna improve reception a lot. See our beginner radio guide for options.
